terms.grammar: adverb; with a genitive, a lot of
evidence: Cic. Att. 8.13.2: multum mēcum mūnicipālēs hominēs loquuntur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: With a verb, “a lot”; with a genitive, “a lot of”: multum temporis, a lot of time.
Above all with verbs of liking.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 15.14.4: ego tibi Rōmam properandum magnō opere cēnseō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: With verbs, above all of wishing, asking, urging and wondering: magnopere velle, ōrāre, mīrārī. With adjectives very rare (use valdē). Plautus, Caesar and Livy write it as one word; the best manuscripts of Terence and Cicero have magnō opere (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: a lot of (an amount): a lot of money, great force
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 2.40: cōnsuētūdinis magna vīs est
terms.comment: For “a lot of” a thing you measure, prose says magnus more often than multus: magna pecūnia, a lot of money; magna cōpia, plenty; magnus numerus, a large number.

terms.gloss: much; in the plural, many, lots of
terms.comment: Multa on its own is “lots of things”, as multum is “a lot”: multum legendum esse, nōn multa (Plin. Ep. 7.9.15). In the singular it is at home in phrases of time: multā nocte, late at night (see late at night).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.7.1: ut tē plūrimum dīligam (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: much (with comparatives): much more, much better
terms.grammar: adverb (the ablative of the measure of difference)
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.48: quī multō plūs efferunt quam accēpērunt
terms.comment: With comparatives and with ante, post: multō plūs, much more; nōn multō post, not long after (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: hesternō, Licinī, diē ōtiōsī multum lūsimus in meīs tabellīs
phrases.english: yesterday, Licinius, with time on our hands, we played a lot on my writing tablets
I liked the house a lot
Lots of things. I play ball.

phrases.latin: an imitārī agrōs fertilēs, quī multō plūs efferunt quam accēpērunt?
phrases.english: or to imitate fertile fields, which give back much more than they received?

phrases.latin: ajunt enim multum legendum esse, nōn multa
phrases.english: for they say one should read much, not many things

phrases.latin: multīs egēre quī multa habeat, magnamque indigentiam nāscī nōn ex inopiā magnā, sed ex magnā cōpiā
phrases.english: that he who has many things needs many things, and that great want comes not from great poverty but from great plenty

magnopere.against: Lewis & Short magnŏpĕrē, marking it like an adverb in -ē
magnopere.html: The ablative of opus, which ends in a short -e like every third-declension ablative: the phrase magnō opere written as one word, as the manuscripts of Terence and Cicero still divide it, and as maximō opere, majōre opere show (Lewis & Short, s.v.).
